title: Circles
description: Identify circle parts and find circumference and area, calculate arc lengths and sector areas using the central angle fraction, apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem and its corollaries, and use tangent-radius perpendicularity.
goals: Identify parts of a circle and find circumference and area
Calculate area of circles, arc lengths, and sector areas
Apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem and related theorems
Use circle theorems involving chords, tangents, and secants
instructionalStrategy: Build from circumference (C = 2πr) to arc length (fraction of circumference) to sector area (fraction of total area).
The central angle is the 'fraction control knob'—θ/360 determines what fraction of the whole circle you're measuring.
Inscribed angles are always half the central angle that subtends the same arc—use this as the 'master theorem' that unlocks the rest.
Tangent lines are always perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency—draw the radius first, then the tangent.

scaffold.title: Circle Vocabulary, Circumference, and Area
scaffold.content:
A **circle** is the set of all points equidistant from a center point. Key vocabulary:

• **Radius (r)** — segment from center to any point on the circle
• **Diameter (d)** — segment through the center connecting two points on the circle (d = 2r)
• **Chord** — segment connecting any two points on the circle
• **Secant** — a line that intersects a circle at two points
• **Tangent** — a line that touches the circle at exactly one point
• **Arc** — a portion of the circle between two points
• **Central angle** — angle with vertex at the center
• **Inscribed angle** — angle with vertex on the circle

**Circumference:** C = 2πr = πd
**Area:** A = πr²
scaffold.initialPrompt: A circle has a diameter of 10 inches. What is the radius? Can you find the circumference and area?

scaffold.title: We-Do: Circle Area — Guided Practice

problems.question: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Find its area, both in terms of π and rounded to the nearest tenth.
problems.answer: A = πr² = π(7)² = 49π cm², which is about 153.9 cm². Keep the units squared — area is measured in square centimetres, not centimetres.
hints: The area formula is A = πr². You are given r directly, so this is a straight substitution.
Square the radius FIRST, then multiply by π: 7² = 49, so A = 49π.
For the decimal, multiply 49 × 3.14159 ≈ 153.9. Leaving the answer as 49π is exact; the decimal is a rounded approximation.

problems.question: A circular tabletop has a diameter of 18 inches. Find its area in terms of π and to the nearest tenth.
problems.answer: The formula needs the radius, not the diameter: r = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 inches. A = π(9)² = 81π ≈ 254.5 square inches. Substituting 18 straight into the formula would give 324π — four times too big, because squaring doubles the effect of the doubled length.
hints: Read what you were given carefully. The formula A = πr² takes the radius, and 18 is the diameter.
Halve it first: r = 9. Only then square.
A = π(9)² = 81π ≈ 254.5 in². Notice the size of the mistake if you skip the halving: you get 324π, which is 4 times too large, not 2 times.

problems.question: A circle has a circumference of 20π units. Find its area.
problems.answer: Work backwards to the radius first. C = 2πr, so 20π = 2πr, and dividing both sides by 2π gives r = 10. Then A = π(10)² = 100π square units (about 314.2). Notice the π cancels cleanly in the first step — there is no need to approximate until the very end, if at all.
hints: You cannot get from circumference to area in one step. The radius is the bridge between them — find r first.
Set 20π = 2πr and solve for r. The π appears on both sides, so it divides out.
r = 10, so A = π(10)² = 100π. Leaving π symbolic throughout keeps the answer exact.

problems.question: A pizza shop sells a 10-inch pizza and a 20-inch pizza, sizes measured by diameter. The 20-inch costs exactly twice as much. Is it twice as much pizza? Justify with area.
problems.answer: 10-inch: r = 5, so A = 25π ≈ 78.5 square inches. 20-inch: r = 10, so A = 100π ≈ 314.2 square inches. The ratio is 100π ÷ 25π = 4, so the large pizza is FOUR times the food for twice the price — a much better deal. The reason: doubling a length multiplies area by 2² = 4, because the radius gets squared. Area always grows by the square of the scale factor.
hints: Both sizes are given as diameters, so halve each one before using A = πr².
Compute both areas: r = 5 gives 25π, and r = 10 gives 100π. Now compare them as a ratio.
100π ÷ 25π = 4, not 2. Doubling the diameter squares into 4× the area — that is why the big pizza is the better buy.

scaffold.initialPrompt: Let's start simple: a circle with radius 7 cm. Which formula gives area — and what's the one step people most often do in the wrong order?

scaffold.title: I-Do: Circumference and Area Calculations

examples.problem: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Find the circumference and area.
examples.solution:
Circumference: C = 2πr = 2π(7) = **14π ≈ 43.98 cm**
Area: A = πr² = π(7²) = **49π ≈ 153.94 cm²**

Key difference: Circumference uses r (linear → length), Area uses r² (squared → square units).

examples.problem: A circle has a diameter of 20 inches. Find the circumference and area.
examples.solution:
Radius = 20/2 = 10 inches.
Circumference: C = πd = 20π ≈ 62.83 in (or C = 2π(10) = 20π)
Area: A = π(10²) = **100π ≈ 314.16 in²**

examples.problem: A circle has circumference 36π. Find the radius, diameter, and area.
examples.solution:
C = 2πr = 36π → r = **18**
Diameter: d = 2(18) = **36**
Area: A = π(18²) = **324π ≈ 1017.88**

Working backwards from circumference: divide by 2π to get r.

scaffold.title: Arc Length and Sector Area
scaffold.content:
**Arc Length** and **Sector Area** are fractions of the whole circle, controlled by the central angle:

**Arc Length** = (θ/360°) × 2πr
This is the fraction (θ/360°) of the full circumference.

**Sector Area** = (θ/360°) × πr²
This is the fraction (θ/360°) of the full area.

Think of it like a pizza: the central angle determines what fraction of the pizza (circle) you're taking. A 90° slice is 90/360 = 1/4 of the pizza.
scaffold.initialPrompt: A pizza has a 12-inch diameter. If you cut a slice with a 60° central angle, what fraction of the whole pizza is that slice?

scaffold.title: We-Do: Sector Area — Guided Practice

problems.question: A circle has radius 12 cm. Find the area of a sector with a central angle of 60°.
problems.answer: The sector is the fraction 60/360 = 1/6 of the circle. Whole circle area = π(12)² = 144π cm². Sector area = (1/6)(144π) = 24π ≈ 75.4 cm². Sanity check: six of these 60° sectors would rebuild the full 144π circle ✓.
hints: A sector is just a fraction of the whole circle. What fraction does a 60° central angle cut off?
60/360 reduces to 1/6. Now find the area of the WHOLE circle first: A = π(12)².
Take one sixth of 144π: 24π ≈ 75.4 cm². Check yourself by asking whether six copies would make the whole circle.

problems.question: Find the area of a sector with radius 6 m and central angle 135°. Give the exact answer and a decimal to the nearest tenth.
problems.answer: Fraction = 135/360 = 3/8. Whole circle = π(6)² = 36π m². Sector = (3/8)(36π) = 27π/2 = 13.5π ≈ 42.4 m². The fraction does not have to be a unit fraction like 1/6 — 3/8 works exactly the same way.
hints: Reduce 135/360 before multiplying — it makes the arithmetic much easier. Both divide by 45.
135/360 = 3/8, and the whole circle is π(6)² = 36π.

problems.question: A sector with a central angle of 72° has an area of 20π square units. Find the radius of the circle.
problems.answer: Set up the formula and solve for r. (72/360)πr² = 20π, and 72/360 = 1/5, so (1/5)πr² = 20π. Multiply both sides by 5: πr² = 100π, so r² = 100 and r = 10 (radius is a length, so reject -10). Check: (1/5)π(10)² = (1/5)(100π) = 20π ✓.
hints: Write the sector-area formula with the unknown in it: (θ/360)πr² = 20π, and substitute θ = 72.
72/360 = 1/5, so the equation is (1/5)πr² = 20π. Multiply both sides by 5 to clear the fraction.
πr² = 100π gives r² = 100, so r = 10. Discard the negative root — a radius cannot be negative.

problems.question: A lawn sprinkler sprays water 15 feet and rotates back and forth through 240°. How much lawn does it water? How much of the circle it sits in does it miss?
problems.answer: Watered region: fraction 240/360 = 2/3 of the circle of radius 15. Whole circle = π(15)² = 225π ft². Watered = (2/3)(225π) = 150π ≈ 471.2 ft². The missed part is the remaining 120°, which is 1/3 of the circle: 225π - 150π = 75π ≈ 235.6 ft². Check: 150π + 75π = 225π, the whole circle ✓.
hints: The sprinkler sweeps a sector of radius 15 with a central angle of 240°. What fraction of a full turn is that?
240/360 = 2/3, and the whole circle is π(15)² = 225π ft². Take two thirds of it.
Watered = 150π ≈ 471.2 ft². For the missed part, either take the leftover 120° (1/3) or subtract from the whole — both give 75π ≈ 235.6 ft².

examples.problem: A circle has radius 10 cm. Find the arc length and sector area for a central angle of 72°.
examples.solution:
Fraction of the circle: 72/360 = 1/5

Arc Length = (1/5) × 2π(10) = (1/5) × 20π = **4π ≈ 12.57 cm**

Sector Area = (1/5) × π(10²) = (1/5) × 100π = **20π ≈ 62.83 cm²**

Both are exactly 1/5 of the whole.

scaffold.title: Inscribed Angle Theorem and Circle Theorems
scaffold.content:
**Inscribed Angle Theorem:** An inscribed angle (vertex on the circle) is **half** the central angle that intercepts the same arc.

If a central angle = 80°, an inscribed angle intercepting the same arc = 40°.

**Key Corollaries:**
• Inscribed angles that intercept the SAME arc are congruent
• An inscribed angle that intercepts a semicircle (diameter) = 90°
• Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary (sum to 180°)

**Tangent-Radius Relationship:** A tangent line is always **perpendicular** to the radius drawn to the point of tangency.

**Tangent-Chord Angle:** The angle between a tangent and a chord = half the intercepted arc.
scaffold.initialPrompt: If a triangle is inscribed in a circle and one side is a diameter, what must the angle opposite that diameter be? Why?

scaffold.title: We-Do: Circle Theorems — Guided Practice

problems.question: BD is a diameter of circle O, and point A lies on the circle. Find ∠BAD. If ∠ABD = 35°, find ∠ADB as well.
problems.answer: ∠BAD is an inscribed angle intercepting a semicircle, so it measures 90° — this is true for ANY point A on the circle, no matter where it sits. Triangle ABD is therefore a right triangle, and its angles sum to 180°: ∠ADB = 180 - 90 - 35 = 55°.
hints: BD is a diameter, so the arc from B to D is half the circle. What does the inscribed angle theorem say about an angle intercepting a semicircle?
An inscribed angle on a diameter is always 90°, wherever A sits on the circle. So ∠BAD = 90°.
That makes ABD a right triangle. Use the angle sum: 180 - 90 - 35.

problems.question: Line PQ is tangent to circle O at point P. The radius OP = 9 and OQ = 15. Find the length PQ.
problems.answer: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency, so ∠OPQ = 90° and triangle OPQ is a right triangle with legs OP and PQ and hypotenuse OQ. Then PQ² = OQ² - OP² = 15² - 9² = 225 - 81 = 144, so PQ = 12. (9-12-15 is the 3-4-5 triple tripled.)
hints: The tangent-radius relationship gives you an angle for free. What is the angle between a tangent and the radius at the point where they meet?
It is 90°, so OPQ is a right triangle. Which side is the hypotenuse — OQ or PQ? The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, so it is OQ.
PQ² = 15² - 9² = 144, so PQ = 12. Notice 9-12-15 is just 3-4-5 scaled by 3.

problems.question: A tangent line and a chord meet at a point on a circle. The arc intercepted by that angle measures 130°. Find the angle between the tangent and the chord, and then find the angle on the other side of the chord.
problems.answer: The tangent-chord angle equals half the intercepted arc: 130 ÷ 2 = 65°. On the other side of the chord, the intercepted arc is the rest of the circle: 360 - 130 = 230°, so that angle is 230 ÷ 2 = 115°. Check: 65° + 115° = 180°, which is right, because the two angles sit on a straight line — the tangent.
hints: The tangent-chord angle is half its intercepted arc — the same halving that the inscribed angle theorem uses.
First angle = 130 ÷ 2 = 65°. For the other side, ask what arc THAT angle intercepts: the rest of the circle.
The remaining arc is 360 - 130 = 230°, so the second angle is 115°. The two should add to 180° because the tangent is a straight line — use that as your check.

problems.question: Points C and D both lie on a circle on the same side of chord AB. Inscribed angles ∠ACB and ∠ADB both intercept arc AB. If ∠ACB = 42°, find ∠ADB, the measure of arc AB, and the central angle ∠AOB.
problems.answer: Inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are congruent, so ∠ADB = 42° — the position of D on that arc does not matter. An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc, so arc AB = 2(42) = 84°. The central angle intercepting the same arc equals the arc itself, so ∠AOB = 84°, which is also twice the inscribed angle.
hints: Both angles intercept the SAME arc AB. There is a corollary about exactly that situation.
Inscribed angles on the same arc are congruent, so ∠ADB = 42° without any calculation.
To get the arc, undo the halving: arc AB = 2 × 42 = 84°. The central angle on that arc has the same measure as the arc, so ∠AOB = 84° too.

scaffold.title: I-Do: Inscribed Angles and Circle Theorems

examples.problem: A central angle measures 100°. Find the inscribed angle that intercepts the same arc, and the major arc.
examples.solution:
Inscribed angle = central angle / 2 = 100° / 2 = **50°**

The intercepted (minor) arc = 100° (same as central angle).
Major arc = 360° - 100° = **260°**

examples.problem: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle. ∠A = (3x + 5)° and ∠C = (5x - 25)°. Find x, ∠A, and ∠C.
examples.solution:
Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral are supplementary:
(3x + 5) + (5x - 25) = 180
8x - 20 = 180
8x = 200 → x = 25

∠A = 3(25) + 5 = **80°**, ∠C = 5(25) - 25 = **100°**
Check: 80 + 100 = 180° ✓

examples.problem: Tangent PA touches circle O at point A. Radius OA = 5. If the distance from P to center O is 13, find the length of tangent PA.
examples.solution:
Tangent ⊥ radius at point of tangency, so △OAP is a right triangle with:
• OA = 5 (leg)
• OP = 13 (hypotenuse)
• PA = ? (leg)

PA² + OA² = OP²
PA² + 25 = 169
PA² = 144
PA = **12**

This is a 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple!
